paras: The assault on Bill Hackney was an attack on a Black man during an affray between white and Black men at Columbia, Virginia, reported in early July 1881, in which he was struck on the head with a pick-handle and thrown from a window fifteen feet above the ground. The incident is known only from a one-sentence wire brief that ran in crime columns of Midwestern weeklies, which gave no cause, assailant or outcome.

According to the brief, an "affray between whites and blacks" took place at Columbia, Virginia, at an unstated date on or before July 7, 1881. During the fight, "a negro named Bill Hackney" was struck on the head with a pick-handle and "flung out of a window fifteen feet from the ground." The report did not say what started the affray, which side began it, how many took part, who struck Hackney, or in what building it took place.
The brief said nothing of the extent of Hackney's injuries or whether he survived, and no report of arrests, charges or a follow-up appears in the coverage.

The item circulated as a single unheadlined sentence in a syndicated "CRIME." column, alongside a Norfolk stabbing, a Mississippi hanging and Chicago forgery news. The Wood County Reporter and the River Falls Journal in Wisconsin and the Canton Advocate in Dakota Territory printed it on July 7, and the Iowa County Democrat of Mineral Point, Wisconsin, on July 8, each in the same words. The column named the race of the injured man but not of his attackers, framing the event only as a racial affray, and added no comment.

reader.title: Assault on Bill Hackney
bases: The only report describes a Black man beaten with a pick-handle and thrown from a window during an 'affray between whites and blacks', with no killing (A1); whether it was a one-sided attack or a mutual fight is not stated.
Every report is the same one-sentence wire brief reprinted verbatim in a 'CRIME.' column (A1, A2, A3, A4); no local or independent account was found.
